1318: The churches of Galatia: either the southern cities Paul visited on his first journey (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe) or ethnic Galatians in the north of the province.
1319: Teachers had urged Gentile believers to be circumcised and keep the Law to belong fully to God's people.
1320: To defend the gospel of grace and Paul's apostolic calling, and to show that Gentiles are children of Abraham through faith in Christ, not by works of the Law, and are to live by the Spirit.
1321: Justification by faith, not works of the Law
1322: One gospel and Paul's independent apostleship
1323: Children of Abraham and heirs of the promise
1329: Agreement in Jerusalem; confrontation at Antioch
1331: The argument from Scripture and experience
1335: Freedom and the life of the Spirit
1336: Works of the flesh and fruit of the Spirit
1338: In his sharpest letter Paul warns young churches against adding circumcision and Law-keeping to faith in Christ. Through his own story and through Abraham's, he argues that Jews and Gentiles alike are made right with God by faith and set free to live by the Spirit.
1339: Accepted everywhere; it headed Marcion's collection of Paul's letters. Martin Luther valued it so highly that he called it his own epistle, 'my Katie von Bora'.
1342: The apostle Paul, writing from prison (Eph 3:1, Eph 4:1), traditionally in Rome.
1343: Disputed. Many critical scholars regard it as deutero-Pauline, written by a disciple of Paul after his death, citing its long sentences, distinctive vocabulary, developed view of the church and close literary dependence on Colossians. Others defend Pauline authorship, attributing differences to a secretary, a circular purpose and a later stage of Paul's thought; scholarly opinion is genuinely divided.
1346: Gentile believers in Asia Minor. 'In Ephesus' (Eph 1:1) is missing in some of the earliest manuscripts, suggesting a circular letter; Marcion knew it as the letter to the Laodiceans.
1347: Gentile Christians needing assurance of their place in God's people and a vision of the church's unity in a pluralistic city culture.
1348: To praise God for the blessings of salvation in Christ, to show that Jews and Gentiles are now one new humanity, and to call believers to live worthily: in unity, holiness, household order and spiritual warfare.
1351: One new humanity: Jew and Gentile reconciled
1352: The church as Christ's body and bride
1353: Spiritual warfare and the armour of God
1356: Saved by grace; Jew and Gentile made one
1357: By grace you have been saved
1359: The mystery revealed and Paul's prayer
1361: One body, gifts for building up
1362: Put off the old self, put on the new
1364: The armour of God and farewell
1365: Ephesians lifts the reader's eyes to God's eternal plan to unite all things in Christ, then shows that plan taking shape in a church where former enemies, Jews and Gentiles, are made one. Its second half turns that vision into everyday conduct in community, home and spiritual conflict.
1366: Accepted in all early lists (Marcion knew it as 'Laodiceans'). Authorship questions are modern; no ancient church disputed it.
1368: The apostle Paul, with Timothy, writing from imprisonment.
1369: Undisputed Pauline letter. Some scholars propose that it combines two or three letters; many defend its unity. The place of imprisonment (Rome, Ephesus or Caesarea) is debated.
1373: The church at Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia and the first church Paul founded in Europe, which had supported him financially.
1374: Paul is in prison and facing a possible death sentence; Epaphroditus has brought a gift and recovered from serious illness. The church faces opposition and some internal rivalry.
1375: To thank the Philippians for their gift, report on his situation, encourage joy and unity modelled on Christ's humility, and warn against those who urged circumcision.
1378: The humility and exaltation of Christ
1381: Thanksgiving and Paul's imprisonment advancing the gospel
1382: Unity and humility: the Christ hymn
1385: Warning and Paul's example: knowing Christ
1386: Loss for the sake of Christ
1388: Exhortations, thanks for the gift and greetings
1389: Writing in chains, Paul thanks his most loyal church and calls them to rejoice and to adopt the mind of Christ, who emptied himself and was exalted. His own ambition is simply to know Christ and the power of his resurrection.
1390: Accepted universally; Polycarp wrote his own letter to the Philippians (c. 110-135) and mentions Paul's letters to them.
1392: The apostle Paul, with Timothy, from prison, sent with Tychicus and Onesimus.
1393: Disputed. A sizeable group of scholars sees it as deutero-Pauline because of its style, its cosmic Christology and its realised view of resurrection with Christ. Many others accept it as Paul's, often noting that Timothy is named as co-sender and that its personal greetings overlap closely with the undisputed Philemon.
1397: The church in Colossae in the Lycus valley, founded by Epaphras rather than Paul, with instructions to share the letter with Laodicea.
1398: A teaching (the 'Colossian philosophy') was pressing ascetic rules, festivals and the worship of angels, implying that Christ was not sufficient.
1399: To show the supremacy and sufficiency of Christ over all powers, to warn against the philosophy, and to describe the new life of those raised with Christ.
1400: Supremacy of Christ in creation and redemption
1402: Warning against human tradition and asceticism
1403: Raised with Christ: setting minds on things above
1408: Fullness in Christ versus the philosophy
1409: New life: put off, put on
1412: Colossians answers a teaching that sought spiritual fullness through rules and mystical experience by pointing to Christ, in whom all the fullness of God dwells bodily. Believers already have everything in him and are called to live out their new life.
1413: Accepted in all early lists, including Marcion's. Col 4:16 mentions a letter 'from Laodicea'; a later Latin 'Epistle to the Laodiceans' circulated but was rejected as non-canonical.
1416: Undisputed; widely regarded as Paul's earliest surviving letter and possibly the earliest NT document. A minority considers 1 Thess 2:14-16 an interpolation.
1417: A young, mostly Gentile church in Thessalonica, capital of Macedonia, which Paul had to leave abruptly.
1418: Written from Corinth on the second journey after Timothy returned with good news of the church's faith amid persecution.
1419: To encourage the church in suffering, defend Paul's conduct, urge holiness, and comfort believers about members who had died before Christ's return.
1421: Turning from idols to serve the living God
1423: The return (parousia) of the Lord and the resurrection of the dead
1424: Readiness for the day of the Lord
1425: Thanksgiving for their reception of the gospel
1426: Paul's ministry among them and his longing to return
1429: The dead in Christ will rise
1430: Like a thief in the night
1432: In what may be the oldest Christian writing we have, Paul encourages new believers who had turned from idols and were suffering for it. He assures them that those who die in Christ will rise when the Lord returns and calls them to live holy, hopeful lives.
1433: Accepted universally and listed by Marcion and the Muratorian fragment.
1435: Paul, with Silvanus and Timothy, shortly after 1 Thessalonians.
1436: Disputed. Many critical scholars think a later writer imitated 1 Thessalonians, pointing to close verbal parallels combined with a different eschatological outlook (signs before the end rather than suddenness). Defenders reply that the differences fit a follow-up letter correcting a misunderstanding, and note the explicit warning against forged letters (2 Thess 2:2).
1439: Persecution continued and some were claiming that the day of the Lord had already come; some members had stopped working.
1440: To encourage the persecuted, correct the claim that the day of the Lord had arrived by describing events that must come first, and rebuke idleness.
1441: God's just judgment and vindication of sufferers
1442: The man of lawlessness and the restrainer
1446: The day of the Lord has not yet come
1448: Request for prayer and warning against idleness
1449: This short letter steadies a suffering church unsettled by claims that the day of the Lord had already come. It points ahead to the revealing of the lawless one and Christ's final victory, and tells believers to stand firm and keep working.
1450: Accepted in all early lists; Polycarp appears to echo it. Authorship debate is modern.
1453: The apostle Paul, writing to his delegate Timothy in Ephesus after a release from his first Roman imprisonment.
1454: The Pastorals (1-2 Timothy, Titus) are the most widely doubted Pauline letters: a majority of critical scholars regard them as pseudonymous works from c. 90-120, citing vocabulary and style, a more developed church order, and difficulty fitting them into Acts. A substantial minority defends Pauline authorship, appealing to the use of a secretary (Luke is sometimes suggested), a post-Acts release and the personal details; some propose genuine fragments incorporated by a later editor.
1455: Pauline, after release from Roman house arrest
1456: Pseudonymous, late first or early second century
1457: Timothy, left in Ephesus to oversee the church, and through him the congregation.
1458: False teachers in Ephesus were promoting myths, genealogies, asceticism and speculative uses of the Law; the church needed sound leadership and order.
1459: To instruct Timothy to silence false teaching, order worship, appoint qualified overseers and deacons, care for widows, and model godliness.
1463: Order in the household of God
1464: Contentment and the danger of wealth
1465: Charge to oppose false teachers; Paul's testimony
1467: Overseers and deacons; the mystery of godliness
1470: False teachers, wealth and final charge
1471: 1 Timothy is a manual for a young leader in a troubled church: guard the truth, order worship, choose trustworthy leaders and care for the vulnerable. At its heart is the conviction that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.
1472: Accepted by Irenaeus and in the Muratorian fragment (which lists letters to individuals as honoured for church order). Marcion's collection lacked the Pastorals, and they are absent from the early papyrus P46, though that manuscript is incomplete.
1475: The apostle Paul, in a final Roman imprisonment shortly before his execution.
1476: Grouped with the Pastorals and judged pseudonymous by many critical scholars. It is the most personal of the three, and some who doubt 1 Timothy and Titus think 2 Timothy may be authentic or contain genuine Pauline material; conservative scholars accept it fully.
1477: Pauline, shortly before martyrdom under Nero
1480: Paul is chained in Rome, deserted by many, expecting death, and asks Timothy to come quickly.
1481: To pass the torch: urging Timothy to guard the gospel, endure suffering, entrust the teaching to faithful others, and preach the word.
1487: Do not be ashamed; guard the deposit
1489: Godlessness in the last days; continue in Scripture
1491: Presented as Paul's last letter, 2 Timothy is a farewell from a prisoner who knows his death is near. He tells his spiritual son to hold fast to the gospel and to Scripture, to share in suffering, and to hand the faith on.
1492: Accepted with the other Pastorals in Irenaeus and the Muratorian fragment; not in Marcion's collection.
1494: The apostle Paul, to his co-worker Titus, left in Crete.
1495: Part of the Pastorals and regarded as pseudonymous by a majority of critical scholars for the same reasons as 1 Timothy; defended as Pauline by others, who place it after a release from Rome.
1497: Titus, overseeing young churches on Crete.
1498: New congregations lacked elders, and 'those of the circumcision' and others were spreading myths and disrupting households.
1499: To instruct Titus to appoint elders, silence false teachers, and teach the various groups in the church to live in a way that adorns the gospel.
1502: The grace of God that trains us
1503: Salvation by mercy and renewal by the Spirit
1504: Greeting; appoint elders in every town
1506: Teach what accords with sound doctrine
1507: The grace of God has appeared
1508: Good works in society; saved by mercy
1509: Titus is a short letter about putting churches in order on Crete. It joins practical instructions about leaders and households to some of the New Testament's richest summaries of grace: God saved us not by our works but by his mercy, through the renewing of the Holy Spirit.
1510: Accepted with the Pastorals in Irenaeus and the Muratorian fragment. Clement of Alexandria and others attest it; Tatian is reported to have accepted Titus while rejecting other Pauline letters.
1513: The apostle Paul, a prisoner, with Timothy.
1515: Philemon, a believer in Colossae, along with Apphia, Archippus and the church meeting in his house.
1516: Onesimus, Philemon's slave, had left his master (perhaps fleeing, perhaps seeking Paul as a mediator), met Paul in prison and become a believer.
1517: To send Onesimus back and appeal to Philemon to receive him no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother, offering to cover any debt.
1519: Brotherhood in Christ across social status
1520: Appeal on the basis of love
1522: Greeting and thanksgiving for Philemon's love
1525: In a single page, Paul asks a slave owner to welcome back his runaway or estranged slave as a brother in Christ. The letter shows the gospel reshaping relationships inside a household church, and readers have long debated how far it challenges the institution of slavery itself.
1526: Accepted in Marcion's collection and the Muratorian fragment. Some in the fourth century questioned whether so personal a letter belonged in Scripture, and Jerome defended it.
1528: Sermon in letter form ('word of exhortation', Heb 13:22)
1529: The Eastern church, from Alexandria onward, attributed it to Paul (P46 places it among Paul's letters), and the King James Version titles it 'the Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Hebrews'. Tertullian proposed Barnabas.
1530: The work is anonymous and nearly all modern scholars, Protestant and Catholic, conclude Paul did not write it: its polished Greek, rhetorical style and the author's statement that he received the message from those who heard the Lord (Heb 2:3) differ from Paul. Suggestions include Apollos (Luther), Barnabas, Priscilla (Harnack), Luke and Silas; many simply echo Origen's verdict that only God knows who wrote it.
1531: Before 70, temple sacrifices apparently still continuing (Heb 10:1-2)
1533: A congregation of believers, probably largely Jewish Christians, who had endured earlier persecution but were now tempted to drift back or give up; Rome is often proposed because 'those from Italy' send greetings (Heb 13:24).
1534: Weariness, social pressure and the pull of the old covenant's visible worship were threatening the community's perseverance.
1535: To warn against falling away and to encourage endurance by showing that Jesus is superior to angels, Moses and the Levitical priesthood, and that his once-for-all sacrifice fulfils the old covenant.
1537: Jesus as great high priest after the order of Melchizedek
1538: The new covenant and the once-for-all sacrifice
1541: The Son superior to the angels
1542: God has spoken by his Son
1544: Jesus superior to Moses; entering God's rest
1548: A better covenant, sanctuary and sacrifice
1551: Run with endurance, looking to Jesus
1553: Hebrews is a sermon to weary believers that argues from Israel's Scriptures that Jesus is God's final word and the true high priest whose single sacrifice opens the way to God. Its repeated warnings and its roll call of faithful witnesses call the hearers to hold on.
1554: One of the antilegomena. The East accepted it early as Pauline (it sits among Paul's letters in P46, c. 200), and 1 Clement quotes it in the 90s. The West hesitated: it is absent from the Muratorian fragment, and Tertullian attributed it to Barnabas. Origen judged that only God knows who wrote it (Eusebius, Church History 6.25). Its canonical status was secured in the West in the late fourth century through Athanasius, Jerome, Augustine and the councils of Hippo and Carthage, which listed it as Paul's. Luther moved it, with James, Jude and Revelation, to the end of his 1522 New Testament.
1557: James, the brother of the Lord and leader of the Jerusalem church, martyred in 62 (Josephus, Antiquities 20.200).
1558: Divided. Many critical scholars think the good Greek, the apparent interaction with Pauline slogans and the late attestation point to a pseudonymous work from a later Jewish-Christian circle. Others argue for James himself, citing its early Jewish-Christian character, closeness to Jesus' teaching in the Sermon on the Mount, absence of developed Christology or church order, and the possibility of a skilled secretary.
1559: Very early, before the Jerusalem council
1561: 'The twelve tribes in the dispersion' (Jas 1:1): Jewish-Christian believers outside the land of Israel.
1562: Scattered congregations facing trials, social inequality, favouritism toward the rich and quarrels.
1563: To call believers to a mature, consistent faith that shows itself in endurance, care for the poor, controlled speech, humility and prayer.
1571: Doers of the word, not hearers only
1572: No partiality; faith without works is dead
1573: Taming the tongue; two kinds of wisdom
1575: Patience, prayer and restoring the wanderer
1576: James reads like wisdom literature for the church: short, vivid commands about trials, speech, money and prayer. Its insistence that a faith with no deeds is dead has made it a test case for how Christians read Paul on justification.
1577: One of the antilegomena: Eusebius lists it among the disputed books (Church History 2.23, 3.25), and it is not in the Muratorian fragment. It was used by Origen, included in the Syriac Peshitta, and affirmed by Athanasius (367) and the African councils. Luther, in his 1522 preface, called it 'an epistle of straw' compared with the chief books (John, Romans, Galatians, 1 Peter) because he saw it as lacking the gospel of Christ; he moved it toward the end of his Bible but did not remove it, and later Lutherans did not follow his low view. Reformed and Catholic interpreters generally read James and Paul as addressing different questions.
1580: The apostle Peter, writing from 'Babylon' (Rome) with the help of Silvanus (1 Pet 5:12-13).
1581: Debated. Many critical scholars consider it pseudonymous, pointing to its fine Greek, Pauline-sounding theology and a setting of widespread persecution they place after Peter's death. Others accept Petrine authorship, often with Silvanus as secretary or drafter, noting its early and wide acceptance.
1583: 'Exiles of the dispersion' in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia, largely Gentile converts in northern Asia Minor.
1584: Believers experiencing social hostility, slander and suffering because they no longer took part in pagan life.
1585: To encourage suffering Christians with their living hope, identity as God's people, and Christ's example, so that they stand firm and do good.
1587: Suffering for doing good, following Christ's example
1588: Identity as elect exiles and a royal priesthood
1591: Born again to a living hope
1592: Called to holiness as God's people
1593: A chosen race, a royal priesthood
1594: Honourable conduct in society and household
1595: Suffering for righteousness after Christ's example
1597: Shepherd the flock; resist the devil
1598: 1 Peter tells scattered, harassed believers that they are God's chosen people, strangers in the world but heirs of an unfading inheritance. Christ's suffering and vindication form the pattern for their own, so they can endure with hope and do good.
1599: Counted among the recognised books (homologoumena) by Eusebius and quoted by Polycarp. Oddly, the surviving Muratorian fragment does not mention it, perhaps because of the text's damaged state.
1602: The apostle Peter near the end of his life (2 Pet 1:14), claiming to be an eyewitness of the transfiguration (2 Pet 1:16-18).
1603: 2 Peter is the NT book most widely judged pseudonymous, by a large majority of critical scholars. Reasons: Greek style very different from 1 Peter, apparent use of Jude, reference to Paul's letters as a known collection alongside 'the other Scriptures', and the problem of the delayed return as a generational issue. Defenders (e.g. Michael Green, Michael Kruger) argue for a different secretary, Peter's own late-life use of Jude, and the testamentary genre, and note that the early church did reject other Petrine works.
1607: Believers who had received 'a faith of equal standing' (2 Pet 1:1), apparently the same readers as an earlier letter (2 Pet 3:1).
1608: False teachers were denying the Lord's return, mocking its delay and promoting moral licence.
1609: To remind readers to grow in godliness, ground their hope in apostolic eyewitness and prophetic Scripture, expose false teachers, and explain the apparent delay of the Lord's coming.
1610: Growth in godliness and knowledge of Christ
1611: Reliability of apostolic testimony and prophecy
1613: The day of the Lord and God's patience
1614: Growing in grace: add to your faith
1617: The promise of the Lord's coming
1618: With the Lord a day is as a thousand years
1619: Closing: Paul's letters and growth in grace
1620: Framed as Peter's last testament, this letter urges believers to keep growing and to hold to the apostolic witness against teachers who scoff at the promise of Christ's return. God's delay is patience, not failure, and the day of the Lord will bring new heavens and a new earth.
